headline: The Race pulling 4 knots on the ebb — albies push into Plum Gut, bass stacking Valiant
subhead: Water holding in the high 60s from New London to Montauk has kept the fall pattern loaded, and the albie run finally punched west into our rips.
body_markdown:
New London is reading 69.4 degrees this week, Kings Point across the way is a touch warmer at 70.9, and that gradient is exactly what's been setting the table in The Race and Plum Gut. Warmer water pushing east against the cooler flow coming out of the Sound creates a seam, and seams hold bait. The Race itself has been running a hard 3.8 to 4.2 knots on the max ebb off Race Rock, with the slack window behind it tightening up — figure it landing close to 11:30 to 11:45 through the back half of this week before it slides earlier as the tidal range builds into the next moon phase. That's your working window at Valiant Rock: fifteen, maybe twenty minutes either side of dead slack before the current takes the wire line and swings it out of the strike zone.

We flagged this last week when the Rhode Island albie run blew up and said it was going to keep pushing west into eastern Long Island Sound — and here it is. Fishers Island Sound has had albies working the rips for several days now, and that push has spilled into Plum Gut and The Sluiceway. It's not a wall-to-wall blitz yet, more a case of pods showing on the surface for ten or fifteen minutes at a time, usually right around the tide change when the bait gets squeezed against the rip edge. When they show, they're eating small — 3/4-ounce epoxy jigs in bone or pink/white, and light metal like a half-ounce Deadly Dick worked with a fast, erratic retrieve. Bonito are mixed in with them off Little Gull and Great Gull Island, same presentation, and the two are hard to tell apart until they're in the net.

The striped bass story is the more dependable one right now. The fall migration is visibly underway, with bass shadowing peanut bunker and mullet schools that are being pushed out of the back bays on the seasonal cue. Valiant Rock and the western end of Race Rock have been holding fish tight to the bottom structure on wire line — 20 to 30 feet of monel with bucktails from 2 to 4 ounces, tipped with a fresh sea worm or a strip of squid, worked slow and heavy right through the last hour of the ebb into slack. That's when the bass stack up on the downcurrent side of the rock waiting for baitfish to lose control in the turbulence. Once the flood builds past a knot and a half, the bite typically shuts down hard until the next slack — this is not a fishery where you can fish through the tide and expect consistency. Time the window or you're wasting drift time.

Bluefish have been the loudest story on the docket this week, and the size class matters — Montauk weighed an 18.49-pound blue in tournament competition, which tells you the bunker-driven push moving through the region is carrying serious fish, not just choppers. That same pattern is working its way toward our end of the Sound as peanut schools funnel through Plum Gut and past Orient Point. Bluefish blitzes have been breaking on top around The Sluiceway on the last of the incoming, and anything cast into a boil — bucktail, popper, or a diamond jig ripped through the foam — has been getting hit within a few casts. If the tidal range keeps building over the next few days as the moon phase tightens up, expect those blitzes to get bigger and more frequent, especially on the last two hours of the flood when bait gets trapped against Plum Gut's east wall.

Fluke have not been much of a story in the deep-water rips this month — that fishery belongs more to Block Island and the open Sound flats right now — but there's still a fair mixed bag of black sea bass coming off structure around Race Rock and the boulder fields off Great Gull on bottom rigs with squid strips, mostly as bycatch on bass drifts rather than a dedicated target. Worth dropping a rig down if the current's too hot to hold bottom with the bucktail anyway.

Looking at the next 48 to 72 hours, the setup favors patience over volume. Squid are building around Rhode Island and pushing into Nantucket Sound as protected water eases into the high 50s, and that's typically the trigger that supercharges the rip fishing all the way down through Fishers Island Sound and into The Race — worth watching closely, because if that squid show pushes this way it usually means bigger bass showing up on the bucktails within a week or two. In the meantime, the smart play is working the slack windows tight — Valiant Rock and Race Rock on wire line through the tide change, Plum Gut and The Sluiceway with epoxy jigs when the albies show on the surface, and staying flexible enough to run to whichever rip is breaking bait that morning. The tidal range is only going to get more aggressive heading into the next moon, which should tighten the bite windows but also increase how hard the fish push when the current finally turns. Get the timing right and this stretch of water is fishing as well as it has all season. Miss the window and it's just fast, empty current.
